hints: Think about the direction of flow inside one single sieve tube, from its source to its sink. Can pressure push the sap both ways in that one tube at once?
Remember that a phloem tissue contains many separate sieve tubes side by side. How could this arrangement allow sucrose to go up while amino acids go down?
walkthrough:
**Recall what drives movement in the phloem**

Long distance transport in sieve tubes is by mass flow, not by active transport along the tube. Active transport is only used for loading at the source and unloading at the sink.

Key rule: mass flow always goes from high hydrostatic pressure (source) to low hydrostatic pressure (sink).

**Apply the one-tube, one-direction rule**

Because of that pressure gradient, one individual sieve tube element can only have flow in one direction at any one moment. It cannot have two opposite mass flows passing through each other in the same tube.

**Explain movement in different directions**

The stem contains bundles with many separate sieve tubes running in parallel. One tube can be carrying sucrose from leaf to root (downwards) while a neighbouring tube carries amino acids from leaf to fruit or bud (upwards or sideways) at the same time. That is how different substances move in different directions overall.

options.A: Incorrect, because long distance movement in all sieve tubes is by mass flow. Active transport does not replace mass flow inside the tube.
options.B: Incorrect, because active transport does not drive flow along the inside of the sieve tube. It is only for loading and unloading solutes.
options.C: Incorrect, because mass flow in a single tube follows one pressure gradient, so it can only go one way at a time, not both ways at once.
options.D: Correct, because each sieve tube has one-way mass flow, but different tubes can flow in opposite directions simultaneously, allowing bidirectional transport.
